title: Scientists Discover “Chunkiest” Squid-Like Creature Ever, Redefining Deep‑Sea Biodiversity】
body:
A pair of exquisitely preserved fossils unearthed from an ancient Jurassic sea floor in Wyoming has revealed a previously unknown, remarkably chunky cephalopod that challenges long‑standing ideas about the evolution of squid‑like animals. The new species, described by an international team of paleontologists, boasts a stout, gelatinous body and an unusually thick mantle, earning it the nickname “the chunkiest” of its kind ever discovered. Its discovery not only adds a fresh branch to the cephalopod family tree but also offers a rare glimpse into the diversity of marine life that thrived in inland seas over 150 million years ago.

The fossils, recovered from the Sundance Formation—a sedimentary deposit that once covered a sprawling inland sea stretching across what is now the western United States—consist of two nearly complete specimens. Both display a robust, barrel‑shaped mantle, short arms, and a well‑defined internal shell (the so‑called gladius) that is significantly thicker than that of any known Jurassic coleoid. Micro‑CT scanning revealed a complex network of muscle fibers and a soft‑tissue imprint that suggests the animal possessed a powerful, buoyancy‑controlling organ, akin to the modern squid’s cuttlebone but far more massive. These anatomical features point to a lifestyle that combined slow, deliberate swimming with a capacity for short bursts of speed, perhaps to ambush prey or evade larger predators.

The find reshapes scientists’ understanding of Jurassic cephalopod ecology, which has traditionally been dominated by slender, fast‑moving forms such as belemnites and early squids. “We’ve long assumed that early coleoids were all relatively streamlined, but this specimen proves that there was a much broader range of body plans,” said Dr. Elena Martínez, lead author of the study and a researcher at the University of Colorado. “Its chunky morphology suggests a different ecological niche—likely a benthic or near‑bottom dweller that relied on camouflage and sudden strikes rather than sustained pursuit.” The researchers propose that the thick mantle may have served as a protective reservoir of nutrients, allowing the animal to endure periods of scarce food in the fluctuating conditions of the Jurassic inland sea.

The discovery also underscores the importance of the Sundance Formation as a window into prehistoric marine ecosystems. While the formation has yielded a wealth of fish, marine reptiles, and invertebrate fossils, well‑preserved cephalopods have been rare due to their soft bodies. The exceptional preservation of these specimens—thanks to rapid burial in fine‑grained mud and low oxygen conditions—offers an unprecedented opportunity to study soft‑tissue anatomy in ancient coleoids. Comparative analysis with contemporaneous species indicates that this “chunkiest” cephalopod may represent a distinct evolutionary experiment, one that did not persist beyond the Jurassic but nonetheless contributed to the broader adaptive radiation of mollusks.

The broader implications extend to modern marine biology as well. By examining the structural adaptations of this ancient creature, scientists can better understand how cephalopods have repeatedly reinvented their body plans in response to environmental pressures. The thick mantle and reinforced gladius could inspire biomimetic designs in soft robotics, where flexible yet sturdy structures are prized. Moreover, the find fuels ongoing debates about the timing and pathways of cephalopod diversification, suggesting that the lineage’s evolutionary history is more intricate than previously thought.

As researchers continue to analyze the fossils with advanced imaging and geochemical techniques, they hope to uncover details about the animal’s diet, reproductive strategies, and developmental stages. Future fieldwork in the Sundance Formation may reveal additional specimens, potentially shedding light on whether this chunky morphology was a localized adaptation or part of a wider, yet undocumented, group of Jurassic coleoids. In the meantime, the discovery serves as a vivid reminder that Earth’s deep past still holds surprises, and each new fossil can rewrite chapters of the story of life on our planet.
